subtopic: STATUS OF VETERANS GUARD, INSTRUCTIONAL STAFFS AND COASTAL DEFENCE UNITS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: STATUS OF VETERANS GUARD, INSTRUCTIONAL STAFFS AND COASTAL DEFENCE UNITS
speechtext:
May I, at this point, reply to a question asked the other day by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). He asked with regard to the 120,000 men of the active army who, I stated, were in Canada. I can say that the veterans guard, coast defence and anti-aircraft units and the instructional staffs at training centres are included in the 120,000.
It is not considered advisable in the public interest to break down the 120,000 by giving detailed numbers in each particular unit or formation, but I hope it will be sufficient for the hon. member's purpose if I tell him that the total number in the veterans guard1, coast defence, anti-aircraft and instructional staffs for training centres is about 25,000. It is difficult to say how many are in each category unless one examines each attestation paper. I discussed the matter this morning with the adjutant general's office, and I think I can say that practically one hundred per cent of the coast defence and anti-aircraft units are in category A. That applies particularly to the Pacific coast units, in which replacements have been made recently, and it applies to a large extent to the eastern coast units as well.
As regards the veterans guard, here again one would have to examine the attestation papers, but from information I have received from the adjutant general's office, I should think that fifty per cent of those would be in category A. With regard to the instructional staffs, it is purely an estimate; one cannot

Questions
say definitely without looking at the attestation papers, but probably fifty per cent of them are in category A as well.
I hope the hon. member and the house will bear in mind that the whole 120,000 are enlisted, under their form of enlistment, for sendee anywhere at any time, and the only thing that would prevent any of them from discharging such service would be, not their will to serve, or the form of enrolment or attestation, but the fact that they did not come wdthin the category now accepted for service overseas.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.

speechtext:
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of National War Services) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 64, to amend the War Charities Act, 1939.
He said: This act was passed shortly after Canada entered the war and has not been amended since. It was not foreseen at that time that there would be calls upon the generosity of the public for contributions to war equipment; consequently the provisions of the act were limited to contributions for war charities. As a large number of funds are now operating whose objects are to purchase war equipment, it is felt desirable that these funds should be subject to regulation. The act was originally administered by the Department of the Secretary of State, but after the inception of the Department of National War Services the administration was transferred to the war services department. An amendment has been necessary to provide for this.
Experience gained from administering the act makes it necessary that further control be given the department if the act is to be properly administered. We have found that in some cases funds have been created without registration and without authorization, and we have no authority under the act to prosecute those raising unregistered funds for failing to comply with its provisions. This amendment now includes provision that will give the department the same control over unregistered funds as it has over those which have been authorized under the act.
We have also found that persons have been holding funds and have refused to make a proper accounting of such funds to the department. An amendment has been necessary to enable the department to demand such an accounting and to secure possession of the funds if necessary.
Proceedings for offences against the act cannot at present be instituted except with 14873-1844
the consent of the minister. As the administration of justice is in the provinces, and prosecutions are carried on by the attorneys general of the provinces, it is felt that the present section restricts the right of the attorney general to institute proceedings where he deems fit. The act is now being amended so as to permit the attorneys general of the provinces to act either on their own initiative or at the request of the department.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
1.	Have any orders in council purporting to change or suspend the operation of the provisions of any dominion statute either in whole or in part been passed since the outbreak of war?
2.	If so, what are the particulars of such orders in council, the dates and the operative effects of the respective orders in council so passed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I might reply
orally to this question. To the first part the answer is, yes. As to the second, I am informed by the clerk of the council that there is no separate index of orders in council which amend statutes, and that it would require a great deal of research to discover the different orders which might have that effect and also to reply to the question as to the operative effect of the respective orders so passed.
What I should like to suggest is that the hon. member who has asked the question confer with the clerk of the council, and perhaps he could indicate specifically the particular orders he may wish to see. He would get a general impression of the position as a whole. I think that would be the simplest way of obtaining the information desired.

The hon. member who asked the question is absent this afternoon. I shall call his attention to the remarks of the Prime Minister. It occurs to me, however, that each minister knows of the orders in council promoted from his department which have the effect of changing the statutes of Canada under the provisions of the War Measures Act, and that in that way this information, which is wholly desirable-I think the public should know; certainly we who are in parliament should know how many orders in council, have been passed, and when, and what they are, and the dates of their operative effect -should be made available. It is a very serious thing to alter a statute of parliament by order in council. I ask the Prime Minister if he will be good enough to have the question followed up a little further and perhaps we can get the information. It is not a controversial matter, but it is one of extreme importance from the point of view of liberty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed that 13,807 orders in council have been passed since September, 1939, and that to obtain the particulars asked for would involve an examination of each one of those orders. I

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think I should answer these questions orally. Replying to No. 1, I can say that the attention of the government has not been called to the dispatch in the Toronto Telegram referred to.
As to No. 2, there is no "Vichy embassy" in Canada. There is a French legation; I suppose that is the institution to which reference is made.
As to No. 3, I am not aware that the British government has recognized any provisional government of General de Gaulle or that there is any such body. That, I think, will answer the question so far as I can do so immediately.
Except as to No. 2.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But may I
say, in regard to these questions which relate to some of the developments in Europe at the present time and which concern discussions that have been and are taking place between the government at Vichy and Germany, that there are no matters which are causing the government of the United Kingdom, and, I imagine, the governments of all free countries more concern than those very matters. I do not think it would be in the interests of freedom itself that any statement which might be premature should be made, or action which might be precipitate should be taken by any government of the British commonwealth of nations at this time. For that reason I hope hon. members will not expect any statement to be made by myself on this very delicate subject until the Prime Minister of Great Britain himself has spoken in reference to it.

Questions
While I am touching on this subject I would say that I noticed a question asked by my hon. friend the leader of the CoOperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) in regard to the position of the French islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon.
As my hon. friend is aware, all islands in the northern half of the western hemisphere have been the subject of careful consideration by the permanent joint board of defence, in relation to both military and naval security; and the government of Canada has been watching the situation closely with respect to such of these islands as are off our coasts. I can assure the house that we have every reason to feel that there is no occasion for concern on the part of the people of Canada in reference to either St. Pierre or Miquelon. I would add that the government is being kept informed of conditions in these islands, also that the government is in constant touch with the government of the United Kingdom in respect to the larger question of the relations between the Vichy government and Germany.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE DATE OF PROROGATION OR ADJOURNMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE DATE OF PROROGATION OR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. I have not given notice, but I do not think it is of great importance, except to some of us, in view of the fact that the housing situation in Ottawa is so serious. Some of us have to give notice now as to whether or not we shall require our living quarters for another month. Would the Prime Minister give us some intimation as to when we may be out of here? I do not want to pay rent for another month if I am going to be here only another week or so.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE DATE OF PROROGATION OR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: I hardly agree with my hon. friend when he says the question is not important. I believe, however, he is in a better position to answer it than I am. I should be very glad if hon. members, through the whips, would confer with respect to the business that remains. I have no doubt if they do that, and take all relevant factors into consideration, they will find some means of arranging for the conclusion of the present stage of this session before too long a time passes.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE DATE OF PROROGATION OR ADJOURNMENT
speechtext: Then may I take it from the Prime Minister that the session will end this week?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):

While we are on this point
may I say to the Prime Minister that I should be happy if he would give early consideration to the question of prorogation or adjournment. I am not indicating any view in regard to the point, but I suppose it will have to be one or the other.

12.	(a) That the provision granting a deduction not exceeding 50 per centum of the net taxable income of any taxpayer which has been paid to any patriotic organization shall be repealed.
(b) That donations to charitable organizations described in the act, up to 10 per centum of the net income of any taxpayer other than a corporation, be allowed, provided that this 10 per centum may be increased to 40 per centum of the taxpayer's net income in respect of gifts to the Canadian war services fund if subscribed on or before April 7, 1941, and paid on or before December 31, 1941.

On more
than one occasion the minister has referred
tMr. Mackenzie King.]
to this provision in the law. Has there been any disposition to abuse the privilege conferred by last year's legislation with respect to large donations to war charities which would have the effect of largely reducing a taxpayer's income? Is there any disposition to defeat the collection of revenue under the guise of gifts to charities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no information on
the point. It was represented to me by those in charge of the recent drive for war sendees that it is extremely important to allow deductions up to fifty per cent of a taxpayer's income, so that many persons would make contributions beyond ten per cent of their net taxable income. I assume that in some instances there would be charitable donations which would go beyond the ten per cent and which, unless a change were made, would therefore be deductible from a taxpayer's income for taxation purposes. But how extensive that practice is, I have no means of knowing.

Then the
minister cannot answer my question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

It seems
to me that the officials of the department might have some information on the point; apparently, however, they have not. The theory upon which they operate, and upon which they ask for this large percentage, apparently was not borne out by the results. The war services campaign was very successful, I believe. It was a great credit to the people of Canada. I suppose it is too soon to look into the future, but if the war goes on another year undoubtedly further demands will be made by the joint services. Does the minister think the reduction in the percentage allowed would operate against the services? If so, it seems to me he might take a compromise stand. This year the exemption in respect of gifts to war services is 40 per cent. The minister is proposing to reduce it to 10 per cent. If he would place the figure at 20 per cent the provision would probably be ample.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I believe 20 per cent would
be about as good as 40 per cent for the charities, because most people do not give more than 10 per cent of their incomes. Certainly very few people give more than 20 per cent. I suggest we should not get away from the 10 per cent, except in respect of corporations.

I am
content.

Resolution agreed to.

13.	That donations to charitable organizations made in 1942 and during any fiscal period ending therein or any fiscal period thereafter by any corporation be allowed up to five per centum of the net income of such corporation, provided that this five per centum may lbe increased to thirty-five per centum of the corporate net income in respect of gifts to the Canadian war services fund if subscribed on on before April 7, 1941, and paid on or before December 31, 1941.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to ask that resolution 13 stand. I wish to examine its provisions in relation to those of the previous section.

Is it
clearly defined in the statute that the words "charitable organizations" include educational, religious and eleemosynary organizations to which we are accustomed to make donations? Is the expression wide enough to cover ordinary charities to which the taxpayer in each community is not only disposed to contribute, but to which he must contribute?
I have in mind, for instance, the Victorian Order of Nurses, a very worthy organization. Is the expression "charitable organization" the generic term covering institutions such as those I have indicated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has always been considered as covering them, and I am told the Department of Justice has so ruled.

I asked not only as a matter of information but in order to allay anxiety, if it may be so described, which has been indicated to me in correspondence. It may be that some are forgetful of or not familiar with the construction placed upon the expression.
Resolution stands.
14.	That the exemptions provided in paragraphs (c),	(e) and (i) of subsection 1 of
section 5 be allowed only if such dependents are maintained in Canada or within the territory composing the British commonwealth of nations or in a country contiguous to Canada; and similarly that for the purposes of national defence tax a taxpayer's marital status and any credit to which he is entitled for dependents be allowed only in respect of dependents maintained in Canada or within the territory composing the British commonwealth of nations or in a country contiguous to Canada.
Why Is it proposed to narrow the provisions of the present exemption? That of course includes the United States. Why the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There have been numerous complaints that workmen and others claiming to be married and having wife and children in certain foreign countries not in the British commonwealth of nations or in the United States were being permitted to deduct from their incomes for taxation purposes as well
as from national defence tax, a certain amount in respect of wife and children. It is generally considered that under the present circumstances this should not be permitted. It is believed such persons should be given these privileges only if their wives or families live in this country, in the United States or within the commonwealth.

Many
foreign nationals living in Canada do not bring out their women folk. I know that is true to a limited degree in my community.
I do know however that they do send support.
I should think most of those men would not be in the category of income tax payers, but all would be paying the national defence tax. The minister no doubt has reasons for the provision, and I do not oppose it.

Would the minister consider inserting a clause which would allow a person whose dependents live outside the designated territory to prove by adequate legal documents that he does qualify? For instance, there are many labourers in Canada from Russia who, I have no doubt, remit funds. There is also a certain number of orientals. The whole of that part of the world from which we have received immigrants has not yet been overrun by the nazis, and undoubtedly there are still some people who could qualify legally for the usual exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman thinks that it is sufficiently important, I shall let the resolution stand and consider it. I do not know just how to handle these sudden suggestions which have such far-reaching implications. I do not see any way of checking on the facts in these cases.
There is no way. So far as I am concerned, I should like to see the resolution carry.

Resolution agreed to.
15.	That any taxpayer, other than a corporation, who enters upon a monthly instalment basis of tax payment on or before the 30th September each year, may pay without interest, in respect of the income of that year, provided, at least
one-twelfth of the estimated tax based on the income of the prior year is paid in each of the months September, October, November and December, and
one-eighth of the unpaid balance of the newly estimated tax based on the income of the calendar year in respect of which the tax is payable is paid in each of the months January to August inclusive.

This is the matter which we discussed briefly a few days ago. The minister is providing for a plan of twelve payments. To this I have no great objection; I believe it would be
Income War Tax Act

easier to do it on this basis than on any other. My personal reaction is that I should like to get it over with in eight payments. Would there be any administrative difficulty in providing an alternative? Perhaps a person could be given the right to switch from one to the other, although it might lead to considerable difficulty. If that is not possible from an administrative standpoint, I have nothing further to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see any great advantage in the other plan when this one is available.

Except
that the people have become accustomed to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This plan is devised to set in, if I may use that phrase, when the other one terminates. If an individual's income tax is raised fifty per cent it will mean that he will continue to pay about the same in September as he paid in August. It might prove a little confusing to have two plans. If a taxpayer wants to pay in eight months, he can speed up his payments; he is not obliged to string them out for the twelve months. He can pay in one instalment if he wishes.
He can wait until March 31 and pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He can wait. I think it would be simpler to have the one instalment plan which can be advertised.
Very well; I shall not press the matter.
Could an individual start to pay in January, so long as he paid his complete tax by the following September?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He must start in September.

Resolution agreed to.
16.	That any corporation which enters upon a monthly instalment basis of tax payment before the commencement of the third month before the close of the fiscal period may pay, without interest, in respect of the income of that year, provided that at least
one-twelfth of the estimated tax based on the income of the prior year is paid in each of the four months immediately prior to the close of the said fiscal period, and
one-eighth of the unpaid balance of the newly- estimated tax based on the income of the fiscal year in respect of which the tax is payable is paid in each of the immediately succeeding eight months following the close of the fiscal period.

This
applies to corporations the same principle that is applied to individuals by No. 15?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

After the change is made as
provided by resolution 11, why is it necessary to provide for these two classes of taxpayers in resolutions 15 and 16? As I understand resolution 15, you simply carry on -with this year's return and pay your twelfth for the months of September, October, November and December. You would then make up your statement for 1941 and be prepared to pay one-eighth of the balance in each of the succeeding eight months. If that principle is to apply in the one case, why should it not apply in the other, so that unincorporated and incorporated companies would all be on the same footing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps this resolution will have to stand; I would have to give that a little more thought. It may be that the two sections are not reconcilable.
I think you must take resolutions 11, 15 and 16 together. In view of the change provided by resolution 11, in fairness to unincorporated and incorporated companies the same ruling should apply.

It is now being made applicable to unincorporated companies, partnerships or proprietorships whose fiscal years end on November 30 or at any other period. I think it could be worked out, but perhaps the minister wants to give the matter more thought. Of course a good deal would depend upon the words used in the bill to be based on the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I can straighten this out, and hon. members who have given more thought to it can correct me if I am wrong. There are two things which we must keep in mind; one, the date for filing the return, and the other, the year in respect of which the tax is paid. Resolution No. 11 has been changed in order to give unincorporated businesses the same time within which to make up their returns as is given to incorporated businesses. That was the point which was raised the other day. I am informed that all taxation years for persons who are not incorporated are calendar years, and if that is correct, these two sections, 15 and 16, are exactly right. The corporate taxpayer may have a fiscal year which does not coincide with the calendar year, but if the unincorporated taxpayer's year is always the calendar year, then it will work out perfectly and harmoniously with the corporation section, to begin with September. But with respect to the incorporated taxpayer we cannot say September. We have to say four months before the end of his fiscal year. The officers tell me that there is no inconsistency

Income War Tax Act
between the two sections. The only reason for saying four months before the end of the fiscal year in the case of a corporation is that the end of the fiscal year may be different from the end of the calendar year. For the unincorporated company the period for which taxes are paid is always the calendar year.
That is an established fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So I am informed.
They will not accept from an unincorporated company a return based on anything but the calendar year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not for income tax purposes.
I mean for income tax purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the individual that pays in the case of an unincorporated company. There is no unincorporated taxpayer.
Then I think the resolution is all right.

Resolution agreed to.
17.	That the resolutions numbered 1, 2, 5, 9, 11, 12, 14 and 15 shall be applicable to the income of the 1941 taxation period and fiscal periods ending therein , and all subsequent periods.
That will have to stand, will it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was an amendment which I said I would move to this section. The hon. member for Rosedale brought up this question previously and the amendment which I read to the committee the other day was as follows:
That resolution No. 17 of the Income War Tax Act be amended by adding thereto the following words:
provided, however, that in the case of resolution No. 9, if any fiscal period ending in 1941 does not coincide with the calendar year, then that proportion of the profits shall be subject to the 22| per centum tax which the number of days of such fiscal period in the calendar year 1941, bears to the total number of days of such fiscal period, and the balance at the previously existing rates.

Some of the resolutions enumerated in 17 have not yet been passed. How can we pass 17 until we have passed the ones to which it refers? Resolution 2, for example, has not been passed, and the same is true of 18.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will let 17 stand until we pass all the others. I would ask that the committee revert to No. 2, dealing with investment income.

Before we go back to resolution No. 2, would the minister explain whether any provision is being made to meet the situation
in provinces where, in addition to income tax, there is also an alternative tax? For example, in British Columbia there is a two per cent gross tax on the production of mines which has been used by the province as an alternate to the income tax. Under the new arrangements between the dominion and the provinces, the provinces are to give up their income tax, but are they also giving up these alternate taxes, or will the position be that where there is such an alternate tax the provincial government will carry on with that tax and thus evade at the expense of the taxpayer the arrangement made with the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is under consideration. The hon. member for Yale asked me that question the other day, and I told him I was not in a position to answer it. It is not strictly relevant to the amendments to the Income War Tax Act.

It is in relation to the
income war tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is relevant to the arrangements with the provinces. We are proposing an increase in the income tax rates and in the corporation tax rates. What taxes we get out of the way through our agreements with the provinces is a matter for consideration when we make those agreements. Many questions will arise, and if we go into them now we shall take a very long time. There is a multiplicity of taxes on corporations in the provinces and there are many which are just on the border-line, so much so that one can hardly tell whether they are income taxes or not. All that will have to be worked out.
That particular point is under consideration at the present time, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

There is one point I should like to have made clear before we go back to No. 2; it is with respect to resolution No. 12. I should like to have it made clear that hereafter charitable and patriotic organizations are to be exactly on the same basis. Is that true?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that will be true.

There are several provisions of this act which will not come into force until such time as the agreements with the provinces are made. Some of these difficulties cannot be cleared up until such agreements are arrived at.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, that is not so. Our
Income War Tax Act amendments come into force whether we make agreements with the provinces or not.
Resolution stands.

2. That paragraph AA of the first schedule to the act be repealed and in lieu thereof there be imposed a tax of 4 per centum on the investment income defined to include dividends, interest, rents, royalties and other like income and not to include salary, wages, fees or other like income from any office or employment of profit or income derived from the carrying on of a trade, vocation or calling.

Will the
minister make clear the present position with respect to investment income, and what the new position will be? From this resolution one would conclude that there is to be a flat tax on investment income without any exemption; but is it not true that there will still be an exemption of 81,500 on investment income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Right.

People
with small incomes who have to pay income tax are entitled, I think, to some slight exemption, and I would ask the minister to make that clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I was going to make
that clear. The hon. member for Vancouver South put the case of a widow with $1,750 of investment income and I told him the other day that I was under the impression that some exemption was provided. In the budget speech, at page 2348 of Hansard I said this:
Our present surtax only taxes investment income within the narrow range between $5,000 and $14,000, and at a low rate. The new surtax is to tax all true investment income of more than $1,500, or of more than the sum of one's exemptions and allowances if these are more than $1,500.
So that there will be an exemption of $1,500, which will be provided for in the act.

Does that mean there will
be an exemption of $1,500 of investment income alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
You can have an investment income of $1,500 before you pay any investment income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Correct.

A widow with an income of $1,800 from investments will get an exemption of $1,500, and the man with an income of $100,000 will get the same exemption and pay on the basis of exactly the same rate as the widow pays on the $300 by which her income exceeds the exemption. On the other hand, of course, he pays the increased rates in ordinary income tax. Is it thought that there is no discrimination in doing away with the sliding scale?

I agree that the arbitrary declaration that all earned income over a certain sum shall be considered as investment income means a hardship in some cases, though not in all. I thought it was a hardship in my own case because I had not been earning very much, but under this perhaps I shall benefit personally. I am not rising, of course, to emphasize that, but I wonder if this will be more equitable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I can explain this any better than I did the other day. As I said the other day, the present investment income tax, so-called, is not really an investment income tax except in a very narrow range
And arbitrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The new scale of income tax was designed really to absorb the scale of so-called investment income rates, and then a tax of four per cent true investment income tax was imposed in addition. All I am making clear now is that there is a $1,500 exemption.
Why four per cent rather than two per cent or five per cent? There must be a reason for four per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there was any particular reason.
It was purely arbitrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; there should be a little differential.
We have at present a sliding scale ranging from two per cent for amounts between $5,000 and $10,000, up to ten per cent. Why was the change made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So as to tax true investment income more than non-investment income. Apparently the large tax the hon. gentleman refers to as applying to investment income was not an additional tax on investment income because earned income bore that tax-all earned income over $14,000. It was considered reasonable that the income tax rate should be applied on earned income and then all the way up there should be an additional tax on investment income with the exception of the exemption of $1,500.
What difference will this make to the revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not possibly tell that.

The minister should give very careful consideration to the amount of this exemption. Practically every widow's

Income War Tax Act
income will be investment income. If she is left insurance, it will be put into investments of such a type that her income therefrom will be considered investment income. On that she will pay regular income tax, and in addition she will pay this investment income tax and national defence tax. I do not think it is fair to keep the exemption so low; I suggest it should be raised to $3,000. At any rate, it should be kept high enough so that the widow who is left a comparatively small amount, whose income is comparatively small and who may have children to support, will not be paying extra taxation. As it stands, many widows will be paying extra taxation, and that is not fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not want to raise it. The hon. gentleman has in mind the widow who has $100,000 of capital invested. At three per cent that is $3,000. We must be careful what we do in such cases, especially when we have high taxes on low incomes. That is always in my mind. I cannot forget it when I am thinking about the taxes on people with considerable amounts of capital.

If a widow is left $50,000, it is a substantial amount of money, but when she is receiving three or four per cent on that money she will find it difficult to pay ordinary income tax, national defence tax, and so on. Many widows are elderly ladies who have to have someone to look after them, if they have no children who can take them in. I know of many who have had to employ nurses to look after them, and the inroads into their incomes have already been substantial. A certain limit should be allowed these people, without putting undue hardship on them.
Mr. FRASER (Peterborough West); Would this include income from annuities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should say so, yes.
Income from annuities is partly income and partly capital. It is partly capital which you get back, because you have to pay out so much money to begin with. It is nearly half capital you get back.
That would apply to any kind of investment.
Don't talk such nonsense.
I didn't know the discussion had descended to the hon. gentleman's level.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member is right. When an investor invests in an annuity the amount that comes back to him is in one sense a return of capital, but the law of the country has always recognized it as taxable, with certain exceptions which have now been eliminated. I have gone over this matter several times in the house and have pointed
out that we had to make a choice as between the British and United States systems of treating annuities. The English courts have consistently held that the purchase of an annuity is the purchase of income. All the yearly payments that come to the investor during his lifetime are in the nature of income, and no separation is made between the original amount of the investment and the interest on it. In the United States a different rule is applied, but the view taken by the English courts and law and parliament and by this country is that the capital has gone irrevocably, that it does not come back but instead an income comes back.

I do not think we should be bound by English law. After all the whole situation over there is different. I have in mind a man who last year sold all his holdings,' amounting to some $88,000, and with the proceeds bought an annuity. Now he is going to be taxed not only on his income from the annuity but on the capital which comes back to him over a period of years. The thing is unfair. We are continually setting up new laws in this country, new systems of taxation. I am not so sure that the time has not come when we should set up a body of men who, instead of having to adhere to some specific legislation as is done in the case of income tax and many other forms of taxation, would decide whether or not this man or that man should be taxed so much. It may be said that if you had such a board it would be influenced by political associations, and so on. Well, the government of the day is Liberal, and when this government passes out, as it eventually will-
What a hope!

It is not a hope; it is an aspiration of the people of this country; they are looking for it. The government sets up courts that have the power of life and death, the power of freedom or incarceration in prison. The men who adjudicate on those cases are in most instances-and I say this regardless of what government is in power- men who have as lawyers paid fealty to the party in power. It is nonsense to say that only the very best lawyers in the country are chosen to be judges. We know something of the men who are chosen to deal with these very important matters. We say we can pick out some lawyer from Windsor, or Toronto, or some unimportant town, who becomes a judge of the high court, and whose address to the jury may either hang a man or save his life, take away or give him his freedom. We entrust that great power to a man who has been in the past an ardent supporter of the party in
Income War Tax Act

office. Yet in matters concerning dollars and cents we say it is impossible to set up a board that will function fairly and honestly. The very attitude that we adopt in this regard results in building up in this country a feeling that government is dishonest and cannot be trusted, because we are prepared to appoint lawyers-
Oh, leave the lawyers out.

We have too many of them in this house. We are prepared to appoint lawyers to these important positions, in which they have the power of life and death over a man, but we are not prepared to set up an organization of business men, honest, conscientious Canadians, to deal with these matters in a decent and honest way and say this is as it should be and this is as it should not be. In fact all the resolutions under the income tax act and under the whole budget system are dealt with in such a way that once they are enacted by this house there is no alternative for the officials of the departments concerned but to say, this is the law. On many occasions they will say, "It is unfair, it is not as it should be, but we have no alternative." I do not know a better organization of officials than those in the Department of National Revenue, the commissioner of customs, the commissioner of income tax, and the commissioner of excise; I do not know three officers in any other department of government who are more competent to carry out their work. The minister does as they tell him. But I do say in all kindness that these men are hedged about by the legislation we pass. They have no freedom, no right to say: "This is not according to what we think is right, but the law says this is what we must do."

There is
always the question of interpretation. They do sometimes stretch it.

They do not stretch it
very far when it is money coming to them, but they stretch it a long way when it is money going from them. We should have some more loosely-organized department; something should be done to give the officers of the department some discretion in the administration of the act. But instead we say, "This is the law; this is what you must live up to." People are penalized one year; at the end of the year we find the whole thing is wrong and we amend the act, but the people are still penalized.
The whole thing is a system of trial and error, anyway.

I still think that having
regard to the drastic tax laws we are now administering, we should have the privilege of setting up a board that would have the right to deal with matters of this kind.
There is always an appeal.
To whom?

you do not frame it by agreement with business, I can say you frame legislation by pressure sometimes, and we had an instance of that in the income tax resolution. I would rather see legislation framed by agreement with business. Why not? Is there anything wrong about that principle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What do you mean by business?

I would say, the representatives of organized business who come here and make a case for equity and equality of sacrifice. Why should there not be agreement? The minister will say, I am sure, that with respect to the income tax resolution many of the amendments he has made have been made in a sense of fairness and justness to business, after business has made the necessary representations. The very amendment with regard to changing the date of filing returns from non-incorporated companies is a case in point. That was done by the minister because of representations that had been made in this house and outside the house. I do not for a moment suggest that the representations made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) or myself were the first to reach the minister on this point. speechtext: The word was agreement, and I said that we did not frame our legislation as a result of agreement with any class or group in this country. We are legislating for the Canadian people.'

I should like to analyse all the representations that have been made and all the promises that have been given by ministers to different people. I could find some instances where there was legislation as a result of agreement.
Understanding.

If the hon. member for Halifax wishes to use that term, I am content. It means the same thing.
Mr. O'BRIEN: When the amendment was introduced in November, I spoke at that time and said that I was in agreement with the suggestion that there should be some flexibility in the dealings of the government with business, business being subject every day to changes and fluctuations, which called for such flexibility on the part of the government. On that occasion the newsprint industry in particular was mentioned. Since then it has been definitely classed as a so-called depressed industry. The Montreal Star, under date of May 3, makes the statement that the Canadian newsprint industry has been declared a depressed industry for the purposes of the excess profits tax. I have here clippings taken from the same paper over a period of time. I do not think it is fair to mention the names of the various companies, but I shall refer to several phrases used in describing their financial position.
It is said, for instance, that one company "shows a wide expansion in sales, in gross income and in net profits." Another shows broad increases in earnings and enhancement in financial position. Another shows that "the profit is equal to $4.14 a share, preferred stock, against forty-four cents." Another shows that "the 1940 profits set a new high record, about S6 earned on common against fourteen cents." Another company shows "substantially higher earnings."
With these statements I have no quarrel because these companies are entitled to earn profits, but it seems extraordinary that while the companies boast to their shareholders of the wonderful gains they have made in their individual enterprises, the industry should be classed as a depressed industry. However, I can see that the two positions are entirely different. But when this amendment was brought in last November, I asked that some consideration be given to the primary producer, who makes it possible in many instances for these companies to function. I refer to the pulpwood producer, the fellow

Excess Profits Tax Act
back in the woods running the bucksaw, either the man making the wood or the man with his woodlot attempting to earn a livelihood in conjunction with his crop. As a matter of fact, pulpwood to-day is lower in price than it was a year ago. I could understand that except for the boasting of these companies that they are making such enormous profits.
In November last, when the amendment was being discussed, I asked that the government consider this matter carefully so that these men might also be looked upon as being to some extent under depressed circumstances. I endeavoured to find out from the war-time prices and trade board whether the newsprint industry came under their jurisdiction. I was told, no, but since my letter contained some interesting information it had been passed on to the timber controller. The timber controller advised me that he has no control over this industry. It strikes me as rather unfair that these companies, because of their power, their ability to spend money on highly-paid legal talent and to send people to Ottawa to promote their case, should be so classed, while the men in the low brackets making the pulpwood are entirely forgotten. Since butter has been controlled, rents have been controlled, and companies or individuals building apartment houses with their own money on their own land are told to-day how much they may or may not charge for rent-

So is industry told what it can spend.
Mr. O'BRIEN: It carries all through except for these people at the far end of the line, who are forgotten. In my constituency of Northumberland and in New Brunswick generally we have thousands of such people, and I submit, since a board has seen fit, in view of this boastful statement in the press of the enormous earnings of these companies-

Since they have seen fit through their board to declare the pulp and paper industry a depressed one, I am only asking that their business be placed under some controller to see that the men at the far end of the line are given proper and necessary consideration; for, unless some change is made in the economic set-up, while this country is fighting to preserve democracy, I am afraid we are going to lose it in Canada.
There is not, so far as I can see, any national policy. We in New Brunswick are practically forgotten. Of all the $300,000,000 odd, collected through this taxation, and contributed by the government as capital to assist private industry-and with such policy I have no quarrel whatever-New Brunswick received only -007 per cent. The new war loan will soon be launched. We in New Brunswick are asked to contribute $10,000,000 of which the constituency of Northumberland is asked to contribute $350,000. I have no doubt these amounts will be reached; but it is most unfair that when our people in that province are contributing as they have been doing to all the loans and the drives for war services-and in the matter of enlistments I believe New Brunswick stands as high as if not higher than other parts of Canada-when we have not these war industries we should be given some consideration to build them up out of the taxation collected from our own people. I ask particularly that the primary producers, who constitute the only industries we have in that section of the country, be given some protection, and that all the protection be not given to these big corporations.

I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to what might be called the level-or, if you like, the plateau -of corporation profits in Canada. I might make an analogy with the order in council regarding labour, No. 7440, whereby labour is given the right to a wage which is at least as good as the best during the 1926 to 1929 period or any time since then, depending upon which is the higher; and then, if the cost of living goes up, every time it rises five per cent they are, I believe allowed an increase.
In the case of corporations I understand that in Great Britain, where the excess profits tax was first introduced and from which place we copied a good deal of our act, the level of corporate profits, or the plateau, in 1937- I am taking that year because I have the figures for it-was 125 per cent of the 1929 level. This is perhaps surprising, but the reason for it is that the heavy industries in the old country were doing extremely well in the latter years of the decade following 1930, their export business had gone up substantially, so that during the period which forms the base or standard profits period in the old country they had a very favourable base, particularly compared with what we term the boom year 1929.
In the United States, the conditions in which are more comparable with those in Canada, I have figures which I believe would be accepted by any authority which indicate that the plateau or level of corporate profits in 1937 was about 67 per cent of what they were in 1929.
In Canada we have no services which have prepared these figures, and obviously one cannot make a personal tabulation of the profits of all corporations in this country. The department must, however, have done some research along these lines in order to impose an equitable tax on industry. To select a base having at least some measure of justice they must have had some figures which throw light on what the level of corporate profits was in Canada during the so-called standard profit period of 1936-1939, compared with the so-called boom year 1929.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; I am informed that
there are no such figures, that on the statistical side the board of referees is trying to arrive at figures which would be comparable with these figures in the United Kingdom and the United States, but it has not been able to do so.

Well, it is difficult to have confidence in a department which levies a tax, borrows it from the old country and does not know whether there is any similarity in conditions here compared with those in the country in which the tax originated. If there is a discrepancy such as the figures I have given indicate, namely, in the old country a level of profits 125 per cent of their most prosperous period prior to the depression, and in Canada perhaps two-thirds-I made a trial of a few companies and I would estimate that the profits during the 1936-1939 period certainly would not be more than two-thirds of what they were in the year 1929, and that would refer to gross profit before taxation; after taxation it would be probably substantially less than that-we should have some idea of what we are doing here. Surely we would not take the wages of labour, without knowing whether or not they were fair, and say, "You must not get any more; you must have your wages fixed at a certain level." In equity and fairness to labour we purposely say, "You shall have the best of the period from 1926 to 1929, or any subsequent period depending upon which is higher," yet we expect industry to accept this tax without question. I am not against it; I merely wish to know what we are doing. The Department of Finance, which is responsible for this measure, must submit itself at least to censure if it is levying taxes without knowing what it is doing.
In my short experience I have found that we are prone to copy the old country, where conditions are not at all comparable with conditions in Canada. We are a progressive country, in the sense that our industries are young and growing, while in Great Britain they have an older and more mature economy. I am sure they would not enact much of our legislation if they were here. On the other hand, whenever it suits our book we borrow from the United States and legislate for a situation in Canada which again is not on all fours with the situation in the republic to the south, although our economy bears a much closer resemblance to that of the United States than to that of the United Kingdom. For instance, just a few moments ago in this committee, with reference to the fifteen per cent ' withholding tax on rentals, royalties and so on, going to foreign countries, we heard the Minister of Finance say that he would look up the British and United States legislation to find out what had been done there. Of course no one has the slightest objection to consulting precedents in these matters and find-

ing out what others have done, but I believe- and I see evidence of it on every hand- that we in Canada lack original thinking on these vital matters.
I should like to ask a question with reference to the words "after adjusting for capital additions". Does that have relation to additions to plant?

I will give the basis for my question. Yesterday I passed a plant where a large addition had been constructed during the previous year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This year?

No; 1940. A man who ought to know-he is not associated with the company, and he may have made the statement without accurate knowledge of the set-up-told me that the same company owned the property adjoining that plant, and that it was contemplating another large addition because, by investing its capital or profits in the plant, it would escape this taxation. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no; they could not avoid any taxes in that way. They would be taxed on their profits.

I have some appreciation of the difficulties which confronted the minister in framing this resolution, but the very difficulties with which he had to contend have left a burden that weighs more heavily on some parts of the country than on others. That is particularly true of Saskatchewan, from which I come. The resolution as amended is much better than the original one, but the standard period is still the years 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939. While the amendment permits the taxpayer to select three of his best years in that period, it is only fair to draw to the attention of the committee the fact that, so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, only one year in that period could be called good, and even that year would not be comparable with the period mentioned a moment ago, namely, 1926 to 1929.
Saskatchewan, together with the rest of Canada, suffered from the depression. I am speaking more particularly of local business rather than of national concerns which are able to balance losses in one part of the country against profits in other parts. A great deal of business in Saskatchewan is conducted by local men and local companies; and by reason of the conditions that prevailed in that province from 1930 to 1935 their reserves were swept away, their capital was impaired and they accumulated debts. The year 1936 was fair, but not at all comparable with any of the years from 1920 to 1930. In Saskatchewan, 1937 was the worst year we ever experienced; I do not think any other province ever suffered such a business setback as we did at that time, when more than three-quarters of the province suffered a complete crop failure. In 1938 we had a fair year in certain parts of the province, and 1939 was generally good throughout.
This will mean that the standard of profits will have to be based virtually upon 1939 alone, and that standard will be so low that taxation will sweep away any profits which may have been made since then. I should like to point out to the minister that the application of even this amended standard period is going to reduce a large number of business institutions in Saskatchewan to a state of perpetual bankruptcy. Like the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. O'Brien), I could draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that Saskatchewan has not been favoured with any war industries. Of the $305,000,000 raised through taxation and

Your fliers are doing great work, too.

Yes, excellent work. Were it not for the development under the British commonwealth air training scheme Saskatchewan would experience no benefit whatsoever from Canada's war activity. Therefore it will be appreciated that this resolution, even as amended, will place difficulties in the way of Saskatchewan business-a business which is anxious to submit its contribution to war appeals and to national war loans.

(York-Sunbury): Is not the basis of this tax as it affects small businesses the cash capital in the business? I refer to those businesses which might be considered as depressed.
The excess.

The basis upon which this tax is imposed in the case of small businesses is the amount of cash capital invested. Effect is not given to the amount of effort expended in the business, a most important but intangible factor. I had some correspondence with a firm of chartered accountants, and they outlined three cases which I think I should bring to the attention of the minister. The first case is that of a man who started up a machine-shop business in 1937. He did little or no business during the first six months, but in 1938 he earned about S2,500 and was able to put $1,000 into his capital account. In 1939 he added another $1,000, and with a little cash contributed by his wife he was able to acquire a total capital of $2,900, with which he started the year 1940. Because of his personal initiative and efforts and due to the increase in business, not necessarily war business, in 1940 he will show a profit of about $8,000. He was able to secure some fairly decent contracts. He will not fall within the category of a new business, even on the basis of the minister's amendment. The criterion set by the minister is additional capital to the extent of one-third. Being non-incorporated he will be able to establish a drawing account of about $3,000, but on the remainder, or $5,000, he will pay a tax of seventy-five per cent as well as an income tax upon the balance. It seems rather severe to take $3,750 of this man's small earnings and then impose an income tax on the balance. According to my correspondent, this man feels that it is not worth while to stay in business when he can get a job which will pay him a larger salary without the responsibility of running a business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amendment would give that man $5,000, so the excess profit would be only $3,000.
He has not put in one-third of his capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolution 5 reads:
That the definition of standard profits be amended by adding thereto a proviso that in no case shall a taxpayer's standard profits be less than five thousand dollars.

But he
will have to pay seventy-five per cent on the difference, plus an income tax. That is an

exceedingly heavy tax for a small business of that kind, and it must be a great detriment to men starting new businesses. I have nothing more to say about that because the minister has pointed out that my correspondent was slightly in error.
The next case is that of a civil engineer who could not find steady employment and who conceived the idea that he might be able to make some money by buying and selling construction equipment. He had $4,000 or $5,000 of his own and was able to get from the bank a credit of $50,000. He started in 1937 and, his firm being incorporated, the most that can be granted is ten per cent on the capital employed before the excess profits tax is applied. During 1937, 1938 and 1939 he made no money, and at the close of the fiscal year ended July 31, 1940, he had just broken even. As a result of his own exertions he has been able to rent a good deal of his equipment for road construction work, airport work and so on, and by July, 1941, he may be able to show a profit of as much as $20,000. In that event he will have to pay a combined income and excess profits tax of about $15,000. The bank and his sponsor have told him that he will have to sell his equipment and fold up, because his profits after paying this excessive taxation will not pay off his credit at the bank in ten years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As a matter of principle, a war excess profits tax act could not be framed in such a way that persons in business would be permitted to pay back what they owe, thereby increasing their capital to a great extent before the tax applies. In this particular case the taxpayer might be able to get relief under the provisions of resolution 9, which reads:
9.	That power he given to the board of referees in the case of both new businesses and depressed businesses to ascertain a fair and reasonable standard profits on some basis other than the capital-standard basis in those cases where the capital employed in the business is so small when compared with the earning power of the business or where other special circumstances of the taxpayer are such that to utilize the capital-standard basis would result in an unjustifiable hardship or would create extreme discrimination or jeopardize that continued existence of the business of the taxpayer.

There is something in what the minister says. The man might get some relief there. But the point I desire to emphasize is this, that the cash capital alone should not be the sole guide. Something ought to be allowed for private initiative, if we believe in that principle at all, for a man's having ability and energy enough to go out and get business and to seize opportunity when it presents itself.

Could some relief not be given to him in the matter of salary? Is he not confined by the provision regarding the amount of salary he may draw for the management of the business? Consideration might be given to that.
I am glad that the minister drew my attention to resolution 9, because I had overlooked that. It gives the board of referees a discretion somewhat similar to what the hon. member for Waterloo South, if I understood him correctly, was arguing for this afternoon. But there is absolutely no principle laid down to guide the board. What is the guide then? Is it to be merely the question of cash capital, or is a man to be allowed something for the result of his intelligent labours? I suggest that there should be something here, some guide to the board of referees in setting up what may be termed a fair and reasonable standard. The language of the resolution is "on some basis other than the capital-standard basis". Why should this not include, to be specific, on a basis of capital-standard plus labour, plus initiative, plus brains, if you will, plus managerial experience and ability? These are the things which I think ought to guide the board of referees. But what is there in the resolution which authorizes them to consider those factors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They may take them into account.
It will not be in the legislation, will it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was waiting to hear language that I could put into legislation, and I have not heard it.
I am sorry that I have not been able to assist the minister. I will give him a suggestion. I will use the term "managerial ability, initiative and experience".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then what is there to prevent all the corporations in Canada from coming along and saying that as a result of better management, as a result of smart work, if you will, they are making far more profits than they did before. When this resolution comes into effect, every corporation will have to pay forty per cent on earnings. I suggest to the minister that to take forty per cent from a corporation by way of income tax and excess profits tax- the intention is really to tax income-is taking one toll from the proprietors and shareholders and then taking another toll from the dividends. When these two taxes are added together, it will be found that the income tax sustained by the proprietors of joint stock companies of this kind is in the very high brackets. It is not fair to say that our income tax is still lower than that paid in Great Britain when we realize that there is no forty per cent paid in Great Britain. The tax on incomes derived from corporations has, I think, reached the pinnacle.

I should like to add my voice to that of the leader of the opposition in protest against this increase in the corporation tax. I do this not with the idea of lessening the total revenue which the country must get, but merely to emphasize the ideas which the leader of the opposition has brought out. After all, a corporation is nothing more than a tool with which to work or with which to provide work, and I do not think it should be subjected to a forty per cent tax before earnings are distributed among the shareholders. This is what is termed a regressive tax and one which is generally considered unfair because it falls equally upon the well to do and upon the very poor shareholder. There is a current idea that the typical shareholder is a wealthy man, whereas I believe that if an analysis
Excess Profits Tax Act

were made of the shareholder lists it would probably show that the average shareholding in Canadian companies is between $2,000 and $3,000. The average is quite small, and the number of large shareholders is also small. If a widow has, let us say, S10,000 invested in a corporation-
She is not so poor.

She may be living on
the income of that, on anywhere from $300 to $500, and that money is to be subjected to a forty per cent tax before she gets it. When we entered the war, this tax was fifteen per cent, and it was raised to eighteen per cent, but now with the imposition of the excess profits tax it amounts to forty per cent on the ordinary earnings irrespective of whether those earnings show an increase over the 1936-39 or pre-war period. It is quite obvious that if this type of taxation continues, the capital value of securities will be reduced to a mere fraction of what they formerly were. We have seen a state of attrition in this country in connection with equity values, whereas in Great Brittain, even with the hardships of the war and the other difficulties they have had to face, security values have shown some enhancement. The effect of a tax such as this will be to cut down the earnings available for distribution. The capital value of a common stock generally bears a definite relation to the earnings of the stock. For example, stocks which formerly sold at $40, earned $2. Now that the tax on earnings has been raised twenty-five per cent, or fifty cents, the capital value will be reduced $10 or $15 a share.
This is an easy tax to collect because there are not very many corporations, and they must pay their bills promptly; but if this type of taxation continues we shall find the value of securities steadily decreasing, and we will have a deflationary atmosphere which will make it extremely difficult to raise money. If this widow to whom I have referred had invested her money in a western farm, her income would not be subject to any tax. But when her money is invested in a corporation, the earnings are subject to a forty per cent tax. I consider this a most unreasonable tax because of the class of people constituting the shareholders of corporations. It is a discriminatory tax, and when the next budget is brought down I hope it will be shown that a steady process is to be inaugurated whereby corporation taxes will be reduced. I should like to point out that if the tax were abolished altogether, earnings would be distributed among the shareholders by way of dividends and the government would be able, by means of the ordinary income tax brackets, to make

its rightful collections to meet war expenses. If, as some of my hon. friends to my left suspect, most of these corporations are owned by those people who pay an income tax of seventy to eighty per cent, then most of these dividends would be subjected to an eighty per cent tax rather than the present forty per cent tax, which would probably suit my hon. friends. I think, if the truth were known, it would be found that the ordinary corporation shareholder is a relatively small holder, and therefore this type of taxation is most unfair.

I wish to make a few remarks on these excess profits tax proposals. Let me say in the first place that I cannot share the anxiety of hon. gentlemen to our right who have been so much disturbed over the excess profits tax as applied to corporations for the reason that in all these resolutions, from No. 1 to No. 18, the minister has taken judicious care to protect the interests of the corporations and other interests who would be obliged to pay excess profits tax; and that is particularly noticeable when compared with his flat-footed decisions with regard to the national defence tax and income tax on the smaller income groups. Do not forget that the heads of these corporations are, for the most part, the people who dictate and write the slogans urging the ordinary people of this country to tighten their belts, and there shall be no profits in war, that this should be an allout war effort.
The hon. member for Rosedale in opening his argument pointed out that the government had been fair to labour in fixing the 1926-29 wage levels as a base and said that

In reply to the hon. member I may say that I am sceptical as to the number of widows who are shareholders of Dominion Iron and Steel, or Dominion Coal, or International Nickel, because these corporations many years ago squeezed out the shareholders with a capital of less than $10,000. I do not think there are any shareholders or heads of these corporations who are asking for as low a return as 310'7 cents an hour, the 1926-29 rate. Montreal, as fixed by Dominion Iron and Steel for their employees. The people who are called upon to pay the national defence tax have no boards of referees and no ambiguous clauses to protect them, but these are provided for the corporations and give them loopholes through which they can crawl later on.
The armchair patriots and the parlour generals map out the war for the ordinary workers to go out and fight it, people earning $660 a year, and it is quite all right to apply the national defence tax to those low incomes. It is not a tax at all; it is taking a percentage of your sweat. There is no board set up to determine whether these people can live on such incomes, which provide practically only the necessities of life. But the corporations are taxed only twenty-five per cent of the excess profits they make over their normal profits of the last three or four years. The minister has not gone far enough; he should have taxed excess profits 100 per cent. These are the people who write the slogans telling us exactly what we should do to fight and win this war and make an all-out effort, and so I say they should be the first to demonstrate that they are prepared to forgo any excess profits in war time. I think the spokesmen of these corporations are ill-advised to rise in their places here and waste the time of the committee to preserve for these corporations twenty-five per cent more profits than they were making prior to the w'ar, because in the final analysis that is what it amounts to. The minister took a step in the right direction when he started to pull the belt tight on the fellow who is not prepared to do so himself.
