Resolved, that it is expedient to enact a Succession Duties Act to provide inter alia:-
1. That succession duties be levied upon or in respect of the following, that is to say:-
(a)	The succession to property, wherever situated, and beneficial interests therein, except real property situated outside of Canada, where the deceased was at the time of his death domiciled in Canada or in one of the provinces thereof;
(b)	The succession to property situated in Canada, or to beneficial interests therein, where the deceased was at the time of his death domiciled outside of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not repeat the observations which I made in the budget debate. The ministry in its wisdom has decided to enter this field of taxation which heretofore has been exclusively a field for the provincial governments of Canada. The only possible excuse for doing so is the need for the money. If it were not for that I suggest that the minister would not propose this type of legislation. When making his budget address, the minister based an argument on the theory that the field had not been exclusively exploited by the provinces. I think that really was the basis for his apologia for entering this field. I suggest to the minister that he must justify that statement, because in my view, and I think in the view of a very great number of people in this country, particularly in the two large provinces, if I may be permitted to say so, this field has been exploited and exploited to the limit and then some. If all the stories are true that one hears with respect to succession duty administration-I lay the emphasis on the word "administration",
Succession Duty Act

as opposed to the theory of the law-there is no manner of doubt about the statement which I propose to make, namely, that so far as Ontario is concerned, the field has been exploited and exploited and exploited-
Mr, MacNICOL: Confiscation.

- and that to-day in Ontario there exists a species of legalized confiscation.
I am not objecting to the principle of succession duties. If anyone cared to investigate the history of this class of legislation, I think they would find revealed an interesting story, that this field was first entered in Great Britain more or less as an accident rather than by design. If I recollect aright, a great chancellor of the exchequer, in seeking to reduce taxation in one field, and being confronted with an apparent deficit, looked round for some other field, and death duties were suggested to him. A very moderate tax was initiated and the budget was balanced by that device. It never was intended to be a perpetual tax on the estates of deceased persons. But the experience of the government in Great Britain was, shall I say, so satisfactory from the point of view of the treasury that from that day to this the field has been covered and re-covered and continues to be covered, and we shall always have this type of taxation. We might as well accept that fact and not discuss the principle of the tax at all.
I do not object to the principle of a succession duty, but I suggest to the minister that we ought not to have two succession duties on the same money. I lay that down as a fundamental principle, just as there should not be two income taxes on the same dollar of income. But before this tax is imposed and levied, an effort ought to be made on the part of this government to reach an accommodation with the provincial governments so that there may be some amelioration for the one taxpayer who is subject to two jurisdictions. Below this measure is proceeded with, or at all events before it comes into operation, I hope the minister will take steps to have a conference with the authorities of all the nine provinces, for I think every one of them has this tax, to arrive, if possible, at some accommodation so that we may not be open to the charge that we tax the same dollar twice and, in some instances, quite severely.
Perhaps I should say a little more on the question of the field. The minister should justify to this committee and to the country his statement in his budget speech that he

is convinced that the field had not been wholly exploited by the provinces. My belief is that the field has been wholly exploited by them, especially by the big provinces, but it has been in no sense overlooked by the small provinces. Those are the two points I desire to make at the moment with respect to this class of legislation.
In my view, before the minister ever introduced this type of legislation he should at all events have made an attempt, even though it might have been abortive, to have a conference with the provinces with a view to reaching some accommodation. In my view there should be but one succession duty in Canada, and that imposed by the central authority. In the first place this would mean uniformity of taxation. In the second place, it would eliminate, to a degree at all events, this terrible system of duplication and, in some instances, triplication, all of which is absolutely unfair, unjust, inequitable and should not be tolerated.
I realize that to deprive the provinces, especially some of the larger ones of a substantial field of taxation upon which they have depended for years and years to carry on their social and other services, would probably make it necessary that some grants in aid should be made to compensate them for the loss of revenue. The minister has incorporated that principle in his income tax proposals, and I have not objected to that. In my view the suggestions made to the provinces to vacate the field of income taxation have been extremely generous. I am glad to think that for the most part the approach to the provinces in that regard has been made in a fairly reasonable manner. They are reviewing the position in an effort to meet the minister's wishes and to see what should be done having regard to the changed conditions that will be brought about in connection with their budgeting for this and future years. That is how this matter should be approached.
Apparently, however, according to what the minister has told us, no attempt has been made to reach any arrangement with the provinces with respect to succession duties.
I beg the minister, even if he thinks he must proceed with this measure, not to bring it into active operation until at least an honest attempt is made to arrive at some kind of arrangement with the provinces. The revenues that will come to the federal treasury from this source will not accrue immediately. It is contemplated by the terms of the resolution, if I apprehend them aright, that no estates shall be taxed unless they fall into the area of this taxation after the passage of the legislation and for a period of six months thereafter. When we come to the appropriate

Succession Duty Act
resolution I desire to say something with respect to that period of six months. Perhaps I might as well say it now.
I cannot lay it down as a universal rule in my experience that six months is too short a time for every estate, but there have been times when six months was altogether too short a period within which estates had to meet this obligation. If anyone has any doubts about that, just let him look back to the period subsequent to 1930, after the crash on the stock market, when the deflation period had set in, when value after value had tumbled from one low level to another. In connection with estates coming within the purview of this kind of legislation, when the time came to pay, they found themselves paying taxation at a valuation more than twice and, in some instances three times as high as the market value of the assets when they came to be liquidated in order to pay the tax. Therefore I think in that respect the period should be longer than six months.
I have no doubt the minister is familiar with the case of the Jost estate in Nova Scotia, which I think was a classic illustration of what I am trying to say. A gentleman having a large fortune invested in speculative securities died just before the collapse of the stock market. The government of the province in which he lived, under the provisions of its law required the liquidation of the estate and payment of the succession duty, and it would not wait. Certain speculative securities, which were the basis of almost the entire fortune, had to be sacrificed; and I am told on good authority that the executor of that estate was called upon to pay in succession duties a sum in excess of what had been realized out of the liquidation, of the entire estate. Consequently the executor, for his own protection, had to apply to the courts for directions. Of course that is an extreme case, probably the worst I have heard of, but it illustrates a situation to which I think we ought to give some attention. Therefore at the moment I am arguing for a longer period than six months.
I have in mind another estate in another province, which fell in at about the time of the depression. The executors were obliged to liquidate immediately; and they were able to pay the succession duty only by sacrificing the entire liquid assets of the estate. That, of course, is an unfortunate situation. In that province the taxing authority refused even to defer the payment of interest; they had the right to take that position, which they did.
Coming back to the original thesis, I ask the minister to take this committee and the country into his confidence and tell us the basis for his belief-if he bona fide holds that
belief-that this field has not been exploited to the full by the provinces; and to give us his reasons, if any there be, why the operation of this law should not be suspended at least until a bona fide effort is made to come to an accommodation with the various provinces either to vacate or at least to share this field.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the need for revenue is very great, as the hon. gentleman knows; and it is the belief of the government that succession duties should be imposed as high as can be reasonably borne in all the circumstances. The succession duty rates that are proposed are not those that would be proposed if we were the only authority imposing succession duties. If we were the only authority, the rates would be considerably higher than those proposed in this legislation. These rates are designed, when the provincial rates are added to them, to be about what the people of the country can reasonably, be expected to bear in succession duties.
Who is the judge of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are in the unhappy position of being obliged to assume that responsibility. The hon. gentleman will note, if he will consult page 2350 of Hansard for April 29, that I said:
The combination of these new dominion rates and the provincial rates should result in a total tax of about the same general magnitude as the British death duties, but with considerable differences in detail due to the different and complex natures of the taxes. The total Canadian rates would be somewhat higher than the British rates on others than close relatives, while they will tend to be lower where ah estate is divided among a number of members of the deceased's own family.
It may be said that this country should not impose death duties as high as the parliament of Great Britain has imposed. It may be said that the death duties in Great Britain are abnormally high, but I am under the impression that, generally speaking, the value attached to the inheritance of property, the maintenance of property in the family, and so on, is greater in Great Britain than it is in Canada. I think the spirit of the people in this country is more to this effect, that as children grow up they are expected to rely upon their own efforts in life. I believe that is true in Canada to a greater extent than in Great Britain, and therefore I think there is considerable reason for saying that these duties are not beyond the capacity of the people to bear, when we find that, generally speaking. they are no higher than the British death duties. That is the basis for the
Succession Duty Act

statement that the field has not been fully occupied by the provinces. The word I used was "occupied", not "exploited." I think I did use the word "exploited" in reference to the provinces, but in reference to ourselves I said that the field had not been fully occupied.

I agree with the leader of the opposition that one succession duty in the country is enough. I believe that the minister should endeavour to see if it would not be possible to have the federal government collect this tax and reimburse the provinces for the amounts they might lose. The question of duplication comes in here again. We shall have these provincial departments collecting these duties all over the country, and the federal department collecting them as well. I believe the federal income tax branch is the proper authority to collect all these taxes. It has all the information with respect to the income tax, and certainly with very little extra help it could handle this tax as well.
One other suggestion I would offer is that the tax, instead of being computed on the value of the estate at the time of death, should be on the value of the estate at the time the tax is payable. I have always thought that would be far better and far more equitable. We would then get away from the difficulty that has been suggested by the leader of the opposition. I know that in British Columbia, in connection with certain succession duty bonds, estate taxes were paid to a point where the taxes were greater than the value of the estate.
One other point has to do with the question of administration. I am referring, not to departmental administration, but to legal administration of estates. Instead of having all these various categories, I believe it would be far better just to have a certain percentage collected on a graded scale, making it as simple as possible so that a man could take care of it when making his will. Do not let the government try to do it for him. We do not need to worry about all these exemptions; it should be done the other way. I hope first of all that the minister will try to see if he cannot prevent the duplication of this tax.

It seems to me that in dealing with a tax of this kind the question of economy should be one of the watchwords guiding the department when making assessments. I cannot help feeling concerned about the duplication mentioned by the hon. member for St. Paul's. I can envisage a huge department in Ottawa dealing with valuations and assessments. I can picture the many technical men in the department required for 
a nation-wide succession duties programme, and I can visualize at the same time duplicate offices, duplicate sets of regulations, duplicate valuators, duplicate assessors, and the train of technical men which will be found in the dominion as well as in every province, who are working at the same type of work. After all, the same set of people have to pay the same taxes.
It seems to me that the minister might very well give some attention to this matter. I confess that matters connected with succession duties are such that the ordinary person does not feel inclined to pass an offhand opinion. But it does seem to me-and I am sure my view would appeal to men in the legal profession in all parts of Canada-that the basis for assessing the tax in the dominion is altogether different from that used in any of the provinces. Certainly that is true so far as Ontario is concerned.
The average person making his will, who attempts to figure out what he will have to pay in succession duties, is in a position where he must do a good deal of calculating, because the whole basis for the assessment of succession duties in the dominion is entirely different from that in Ontario. For instance, the exemptions are quite different; the rates are entirely different; the whole structural set-up is entirely different from that to which he has been accustomed. That is one point which has occurred to me.
Here is another angle. I suggest that the minister ought to tell the committee what the estimated cost of the new department is going to be; it seems to me there must be some estimate. He should also tell us whether he has given due consideration to the point as to whether additional percentages might have been added to the already existing succession duties schedule structure in the various provinces. Had that been done, we would at least have had some .yardstick to go by in our calculations with respect to succession duties. The minister's answer may be that it would mean in some provinces a differentiation in favour of others. Surely, however, there must be some wa37 of avoiding an expensive duplication of departments.
Before the war broke out, there was a consuming desire on the part of taxpayers across Canada to do away with duplications. There was scarcely a newspaper having any influence which did not say that there was too much duplication of government. It was pointed out that there was duplication of departments. Surely, in a time of war, when everybody is saving to the limit, we should exercise the most extreme caution to see that in the collection of new taxes we are not setting up additional expensive departments.

Succession Duty Act
There must be no overlapping with those departments already operating to collect taxes for the various provinces. I suggest that the minister might give serious consideration to the point I have made. I mention these matters only with the idea of trying to save Canada some money. After all, in these times, when we need every cent we have, there must be some solution. It ought not to be necessary to set up a new department which will do the same kind of work, and which will only duplicate the work already done by the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know how to adopt the suggestions which have been made. It has been suggested that we should now get in touch with the provinces, or that before this we should have got in touch with them and tried to get them out of the succession duties field. If one thing was made clear at the conference held in January, it was this, that any encroachment on the provincial field by the dominion, which would be agreed to by the provinces, would be agreed to only for the period of the war.
When one is dealing with succession duties he cannot act temporarily, because it would be most unfair to do so. It would mean that the estates of those people who died within a certain period of time would be subjected to a certain rate or level of taxation. On the other hand, other estates would not be subjected to the same tax.
It would be better to live until after the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rules which apply in Tespect of succession duties do not apply to income and corporation taxes, which are annual and recurring.
Did I understand the minister to say that the provinces were agreeable to the dominions taking over the entire collection of succession duties during the period of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; they never got that far-or within a thousand miles of it. What I said was that anything they might do would be only for the period of the war. That, of course, did not apply to all the provinces, but it applied to enough of them to make it impossible to hope to get the succession duties wholly in the hands of the dominion government. Therefore we just had to adapt ourselves to the situation.
We are imposing succession duties, and wall continue to impose them. We do not intend to stop imposing them at the conclusion of the war. From our point of view this is not a temporary tax.
When you can get it so easily, you will keep it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether or not we will get it easily, but we have no intention of just taking the estates of people who die in the next two or three years, and letting people who die afterward go free.
Will the legislation apply to a person who died about six years ago, but whose will has not yet been probated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It applies only to deaths after the passage of the legislation.

Perhaps
the minister overlooked it, but he has not yet replied to my suggestion that there should be a conference with the provinces with respect to this tax. Again I remind him that at the conference in January, the premier of Ontario intimated that he had well-equipped machinery, if I may put it in that way, for the collection of succession duties, and that he would be glad to place it at the disposal of the federal authorities. He might have had his tongue in his cheek at the time he made that offer, but it may be that I have misjudged the gentleman. I would point out, however, that there will be a duplication of effort and expense, and that the cost of collecting these two succession duties, and, in some instances, three-I can give the minister instances where there will be three taxes on the same dollar-will be great. If the Dominion of Canada has to set up machinery to collect succession duties, I think it will be found that the cost of collection will be much greater than the cost of collecting the income tax.
This type of taxation opens up the whole field of value which in Ontario has been carried to an absurd extreme. Let me give the minister an example of what has happened in this province. A testator died, and his executors filed an inventory and the ordinary affidavits required by the act. A number of officials swarmed down upon the testator's home and went through the jewellery, the cutlery, the silverware, the chinaware and all the other items. They went to the sideboard, and they said, "here is a sterling silver dish; put down $100," whereas it was a plated piece worth about $5. That actually happened in the city of Ottawa, and it will happen again unless great patience is displayed by the executors or those representing estates. To me such a thing is simply scandalous.
I can give the minister another illustration. Not so long ago there died in this country a great statesman who during his lifetime had been the recipient of various marks of
Succession Duty Act

respect and appreciation by foreign governments, municipalities and so on. Those tokens of respect took the form of caskets and that sort of thing, having no real commercial value. However, to the family of the deceased they had what we might term a price of affection or a price of sentiment, but arbitrary valuations were placed upon all these articles. To me such a procedure is simply shocking, and if the general public knew what was going on they would never approve it. I do not care what demagogue gets up and says, "soak the rich," which is the theory behind all these activities; it should not be done. I hope there will be nothing of that sort attaching to this new department of taxation and government.
I do not think the minister has met the case which I suggested to him. He has said that the rates here will be no greater than those applying in Great Britain. They should not be. This is a young country, and we have not the accumulated wealth that they have in the motherland. This legislation contemplates taxation of estates down to $5,000 in value under certain circumstances. That is a pretty low limit, so low that I venture to say that in the final result the cost of collecting in the case of these small estates will be greater than the return. Stacks of cordwood will have to be counted in order to decide whether an estate is under or over $5,000. For years, $50,000 was the limit, but because of the increase in social services this was reduced to 825,000, I think in all provinces. I suggest to the minister that no estate under 825,000 should be taxed, unless it be one where there are no blood relations involved. After all, that would be a small estate. When we come to the proper resolution, I hope the minister will tell us that he is giving some consideration to this matter.
This will mean a double expense. If there was just the one succession duty levied, there would be some saving to the people who have to pay. I am appalled at the idea that in all these measures of taxation no one seems to have given any consideration to the taxpayer. This all seems to be based upon the principle of what the traffic will bear, or how much money we can get. No consideration is being given to the individual person whose patrimony is being passed on to the state under the guise of legal taxation which, in many instances, amounts to pure confiscation.
I am not going to argue against the principle, but in my view this field has been fully occupied and exploited in a country as young as Canada. We have no great accumulation of invested wealth which has been passed on from generation to generation. Most of the wealth of this dominion is the result of efficiency and thrift and the application of good

business principles on the part of the testator involved. We ought not to penalize these people too much. There is a trite saying that in Canada and the United States it is shirtsleeves to shirt-sleeves in two generations.
What is wrong with that?

My hon. friend bo my left would not understand the argument I am making, and I am not going to address myself to him. Individuals with socialistic tendencies who have nothing themselves do not seem to want anyone else to have anything. They want to take from those who have; they want to penalize thrift, efficiency and all the other virtues which make up the best type of citizenship that we have in this country.
Restore to the people the resources that belong to them.

That is the kind of claptrap I have been hearing in this house for twenty years. This is not a socialist state, and so long as I have a seat in this house and a voice to make my opinions heard, it will not be. I venture to say that if you took the accumulated wealth in this country, if you took from those who have and distributed it among those who have not, in less than a generation it would get back to its original source. The others simply have not the efficiency and ability to hang on to anything.
What does the hon. member mean by wealth?

I am not going to be side-tracked into a discussion of wealth. There is material wealth and there are other types of wealth. I do not wish to labour this question any longer except to say that this type of legislation is going to destroy every incentive for thrift, a thing that should govern the lives of the people of any country. If you do not have thrift; if you do not have people laying up something for their old age-and this legislation will discourage them-then, of course, we might as well prepare to get into the old age pension class as soon as possible.

I plead with the minister to make some effort to see to it that when the measure is in operation, every possible means shall be used to avoid duplication in the cost of administering estates. I remember last winter, or maybe it was a year or two ago, a certain estate in Ottawa was under investigation for some length of time. The Ontario government had a large staff living at the Chateau Laurier in expensive

Succession Duty Act
rooms and eating daily three expensive meals. They were there a long time, and it must have cost a lot of money. I met these same gentlemen in various places in Ontario investigating estates. As I sat listening to my leader pleading for some means to give fair play to estates, I was wondering what the result would be if three different groups of men, one from the Ontario government, one from the federal government and perhaps a third from some other provincial government, were at the Chateau Laurier for perhaps a month or two, or perhaps longer, investigating the same estates. Whoever might die and leave an estate, if he came back from his grave would use strong language against men investigating estates under those circumstances. As my leader said, it will not be worth while for anyone to try to save a dollar if estates are to be investigated by several governments, all inquiring into the same estate, as I have seen around the Chateau Laurier in the last few years.

I would not be so much concerned about the large numbers congregated at the Chateau Laurier as I would be about another angle that occurs to me. With regard to an estate that has assets in Saskatchewan and in Ontario, paying duties in both provinces, as estates often do, and also paying to the dominion government, what are you going to do should the valuators arrive at different valuations? You will not get a valuator representing the Saskatchewan government, a second one representing the dominion government, and another representing the Ontario government all arriving at the same valuation in one case out of a hundred. When you reach that point, you are going to create a disturbing situation so far as executors and beneficiaries are concerned, because if different valuations are arrived at, I cannot imagine anything that would be more fatal to the general administration of estates and the collection of duties than such a state of affairs. That is one reason why I have argued for some elimination of duplication in connection with assessment and valuation for duty purposes, and the minister might properly answer the question I asked previously as to what will be the estimated cost of this department per annum, or at its inception in any event, because, as we go along, the expense will be greater. We should know what the estimated cost per annum of the succession duty department in Canada will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No estimate has been made. We have no experience to go on.

That bears out what we have been saying. Surely the minister does
not seriously come to the committee and say that he will collect 820,000,000 of succession duties a year and that he has not even an estimate of what it will cost to collect this sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
That is a serious position for the minister to take.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why?

Is it going to cost twenty, or ten or five millions or one million? The minister must have some kind of estimate. I am not asking for an estimate that is within ten or fifteen hundred dollars. I am asking for some idea of the percentage of money collected that will go into administration and collection charges, and I think the committee is entitled to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No estimate has been made.

Has the minister visualized any set-up of an organization? Does he propose to have a superintendent in every province or, in the larger provinces, more than one, something after the system of the income tax? Does he propose to have auditors travelling round the country making reports, or inspectors or whatever they may be called? Or maybe he will have both auditors and inspectors, because an inspector might not be capable of auditing books. My recollection is that most of the disagreements in arriving at valuations of estates are with regard to values placed by succession duty authorities on what might be termed family companies or closed corporations held by the testator and his immediate relatives or his immediate entourage. Those shares may not have any market value at all; they may never have established a market value. Recourse must be had, therefore, to book values, valuation of assets, deductions of liabilities and so forth. What does the minister contemplate in the shape of a set-up? Surely that is a reasonable question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is pretty much all there now. The income tax division has a head office at Ottawa; there are a large number of district offices of the income tax division all over Canada, and the matter will be handled largely from these income tax offices.

Is it expected that the inspectors in the various provinces are capable of handling succession duty matters without experience at all? They have not had experience, and some do not know much about income tax. If you go to them now and ask them what this
Succession Duty Act

means in the budget, they will throw up their hands and say, "We don't know; we shall have to wait until we hear from
Ottawa." That has happened in the last few weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are some pretty
good men.

On the
whole, there are some good men.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are intelligent men doing a pretty good job, and I have no doubt they will be able to handle this. The provinces have been able to handle it.

They
had to train men.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They did not wait to train them before they passed their acts, and neither shall we.

When
these acts went into force in 1892, in my province the matter was handled by the attorney general himself and he took a commission for it. If the committee wishes to know who he was, he was the late lamented William Pugsley, and he took for himself a commission on the settlement of these estates over and above his salary as attorney general, or whatever his position was in the government.
That was the law of the country.
He made the law. It is easy enough to answer me that. I never suggested that it was illegal, but, even if he is gone, I say it was a scandalous law set up by a man who profited by it himself.
And his successors continued it.

Not very long, not in my time. I know that away back in 1892 it was a relatively small job to settle succession duties in New Brunswick, because the estates that were taxed were limited to those of $50,000 and over, and there were not many in those days. In fact, there are not so many now. I suggest to the minister that he will have to have some kind of staff which has had experience with succession duty laws. Heretofore it has been a complex field of jurisprudence. Anyone who does not believe that has only to look over the decisions rendered from time to time by the privy council and the high courts in Canada. It is a complex field of jurisprudence and has given rise to a great
[Mr. R. B. Hanson.l
deal of litigation, and very expensive litigation too. I suggest that you cannot just put the ordinary accountant into this field and have him make a success of it. .

The minister was unable to give us any kind of estimate of the cost of administration. Will he be good enough to tell us whether his estimate of $20,000,000 of revenue to be derived from these duties was a gross or net estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Gross.

We have been given no
conception yet of what the net return from these succession duties is going to be, because we have not the slightest guide from the minister as to what the cost of collecting the $20,000,000 will be. Therefore the minister might just as well have never made his estimate of $20,000,000 in the first place. Can he give us some idea of the number of additional employees who will be required in the dominion income tax division to handle the additional amount of work involved in the collection of succession duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; I cannot give the
number. When my hon. friend says that I should be in a position to give an estimate-
I think you should.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-of the cost of collection,
I think I can safely say that it will be less than five per cent, probably three or two per cent or thereabouts, but no attempt was made to ascertain that figure. We know in all reason that it will not be very great, but there is no use in making an estimate like that. We shall do it as cheaply as we can. We know that it is a productive tax in the province, and it is likely to be so here. The main task is the valuing of the property, and the income tax staff has had a great deal of experience in that work. They are continually valuing assets and liabilities. It is not such a terribly difficult thing to do. My hon. friends opposite who are setting up such terrific difficulties-

We know because we
have lived in Ontario for many years.

The minister may find
out about the difficulties when he gets into this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no reason to think
the difficulties are insurmountable or even formidable, and I do not think my hon. friends opposite have any reason for thinking so.

I do not think the minister knows much about it, to tell the truth.

Succession Duty Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree that I do not know a great deal about it, but I am confident that I know just as much about it as any hon. gentleman opposite who has spoken. This is an explored field in which the provincial governments have been collecting the tax for quite a long time, and apparently with great success, and it stands to reason it is not something we should shrink from with fear, as hon. gentlemen opposite are apparently doing.
I should like to know what they would do in solving some of the problems we have to solve in the war field if they are so afraid of difficulties in putting into force a comparatively simple piece of fiscal legislation such as this.

We are
not afraid. The reaction on the minister is not exactly what I thought it would be. We have not shrunk and nobody will shrink from applying the tax, but we think the minister ought to give us more information. Upon what was the gross estimate of $20,000,000 based? Was it upon the returns to the various provinces? They must have knowledge of the returns, and I cannot imagine any other measure by which the minister could arrive at the gross estimate of $20,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was based on the succession duty revenues of the provinces and a comparison of the proposed rates with the provincial rates.

The minister ought to be able to give us some idea of the cost of administration. We have had succession duties in Ontario for many years, and all the minister would need to do would be to telephone Toronto and ask the government how much succession duty revenues they took in during a year and how many employees were required to administer the act in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not imagine anything more fruitless than tr}'ing to estimate the cost of administration of this measure. We shall know in a year what the cost will be, and I am sure it will not be very great in proportion to the total amount collected.

I hope the minister will not reconsider this important piece of legislation as the result of the protests from hon. gentlemen to my right. Here is one field of taxation which will provide a good deal of revenue, and it will come from people to whom Canada has been extremely kind. I noted what the leader of the opposition said about people who have accumulated considerable fortunes as a result of thrift, and there is a good deal to be said for those who. as a result of
hard work, accumulate a fortune. But is that any reason why they should pass it on to their children and grandchildren? I think Canada has a real claim, particularly at the present time, to an even higher share than is provided here of these large fortunes. I have a clipping here which was on my desk relating to the death of one of the greatest Canadians of our generation, Sir Frederick Banting, who made one of the greatest contributions to the world in the present century, but who left a very small estate. Men in other fields who are making a much smaller contribution to the world's progress are leaving very large estates as a result of their activities.
How can you know how much a man leaves?
The information is available. The estate was $72,300.
I am glad to hear the hon. member say that that is a small estate.

It is very small according to this press clipping dated Toronto, March 31.
The leader of the opposition has referred to people who are very thrifty and suggested that these succession duties may take away the incentive to thrift. I represent a constituency where the people are as thrifty as people anywhere in this dominion; yet hardly one per cent of them are going to pay any income tax, and very few of them will leave estates to be taxed for succession duties. They will not have estates to leave to be whittled away.
I think the leader of the opposition gives a wrong impression when he suggests that members in this corner of the house wish to make a pile of all the wealth of Canada and divide it up into equal portions. The wealth of the world is something which one cannot divide once and for all. It is produced day by day and hour by hour. It is created as a result of people applying human labour to the natural resources which are our common heritage. We should like to see all the people of Canada have the right to apply labour to our raw materials and to have a fair share of the wealth which is created through the cooperative efforts of all the people. This wealth is not consumed once and for all. It is created day by day and consumed day by day, as our factories are working, as our trains are moving goods from one part of the country to another, transporting the new wealth that has been created from one area to another. No, Mr. Chairman, we do not wish to divide the wealth of Canada
Succession Duty Act

once and for all, but we d.o wish to see the people of Canada get a fair share of the wealth that is distributed.
I hope the minister will increase these succession duties, particularly on the larger estates. Take a fortune like the Astor estate in the United States. An immigrant came to the United States and bought some land in an area that was not then very popular. He was not responsible for the millions of people who afterwards came to make up the city of New York. Had Astor gone to my constituency and bought a tract of land there, he would find himself with a serious liability to-day.
He would become a C.C.F.-er.

I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that it is not fair that the descendants for all time to come of this original settler on some land in New York city should enjoy that huge fortune without making some contribution to the state, and so in Canada it is hardly fair that the children of even those who perform outstanding services should be permitted to go through life with riotous living, enjoying the very cream of our production, without being required to perform some useful service to society. This tax is to be commended, and the rates should be increased, especially for the larger amounts.

Regarding succession duty and this resolution about imposing certain duties on the same class of property as the provinces are taxing, I am not at all surprised at these phantom resolutions of the minister and the phantom methods of the department to save the dollar. I remember when this class of assessment of property was introduced in Ontario in the days of Sir Oliver Mowat. There was a long discussion between the Department of Justice and others about certain points. One was the public policy of assessing certain property of those domiciled within the jurisdiction, making an effort to cover property of those not within the jurisdiction. Cases went to the privy council on it. There have been some cases dealing with that particular problem.
We have now a war on. If the government are going to adopt this principle and upset sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act regarding property and civil rights in the provinces and the municipalities-for they get a share of this indirectly-the whole principle is all wrong. Every tax must have a principle. We might just as well abolish the provinces. Is this parliament sitting here going to usurp the rights and powers of the provinces without the consent of the people

and take all classes of property and assess it for succession duty? Hon. gentlemen opposite wanted to give the provinces a sales tax. Resolution 1 is against principles of all public policy. Where did this particular resolution come from and who recommended it? The provinces were not consulted. I doubt whether, notwithstanding the War Measures Act, this parliament has power to impose a system of taxation outside its jurisdiction, extra-territorially. I also object on the grounds of public policy to this conflict of law by this highway robbery principle of taxation without the consent of the people. It upsets the whole basis on which confederation was founded and the taxation powers of the provincial system, and the municipal system. It takes away all the sources of revenue of the municipalities except the tax on real estate. The government now comes to the provinces and makes a raid on almost every item of section 92, property and civil rights in the provinces. The government might just as well abolish the provinces; that is where they are headings, for the totalitarian state and the Marxian system.
This matter was discussed for many years, and it was found that the provinces and municipalities had a right to live. The principle of live and let live has been forgotten in this raid on the revenues, trying to bolster up the dollar. If the government had been as anxious to qualify under the lease-lend bill, they could have got somewhere; we would not have half the present budget, and hundreds of millions of dollars could be supplied to Great Britain and financed by a loan at one-half or two-thirds of one per cent. But the country is not going to stand for the present system that is being inflicted upon the municipalities and the provinces. The court of last resort, the voice of the people, will decide whether this parliament shall upset the whole basis of confederation and impose a system of taxation which is not within its power to impose.
Under the Ontario succession duties act, if a man is killed on active service, his estate is excluded from the tax. Does that apply here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. A provision is made
for a lower value than otherwise would be the case, something similar to the provision in the English succession duties act. But it is not exempt altogether.

Is any
provision to be made for amelioration in the case of quick succession?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.

Succession Duty Act

I suggest that in all equity and fairness some consideration ought to be given to making allowance for what is known as quick succession. A man dies; he has $50,000; he leaves it to his wife; within six months she dies, and it passes to someone else and is taxed again.
I have seen this happen within a year. New Brunswick has recognized the principle of quick succession and has taken authority to ease the burden by order in council. They have to be satisfied by a specific statement of the facts under oath as to what the position is. I have always thought it a fair provision to have in the law. I ask the minister to give some consideration to that. If he will examine the statutes in certain jurisdictions-
I am not prepared at the moment to say which ones-he will find that consideration has been given to that theory.
I have said all I intend to say on the general principle. The theory of this tax is that it is based on the succession to property, as distinguished from a tax on property itself. The minister wall recall that the old theory of the laws in the various provinces was based on the power to levy direct taxation on property within the province. Various attempts were made from time to time to extend that theory, and in one jurisdiction at least I recall that the government of the day passed a law declaring that property descending from an estate of a testator in one province to recipients in another province was property within the province to which it was being transferred by the effect of the will. That is to say, it wras declaring property to be property within the province which was not property within the province. For many a day I ached to get a chance to expose that fallacy. But I never got a real chance to contest the constitutionality of that position. About 1932 a case went from Alberta to the privy council which gave me great satisfaction. It probably wiped out the opportunity I had to fight a principle which I had been contesting before the provincial authorities for years. It put a new complexion on the whole position.
As a result of that judgment, the provinces all got together and passed new succession duty acts, and they finally united on the theory that the main tax would be levied on the succession. That is what the minister has decided to do in this instance. But that is not necessary in the case of a dominion act. The tax under a dominion act should be levied on the property passing from a testator domiciled in the country, but excluding real estate outside the jurisdiction of the federal
authority. What has the minister to say about those two distinctions, because here it is plainly indicated by the resolution that the tax is to be on the succession, not on property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I understand the point. If the hon. gentleman is suggesting that we should base our legislation on the principle of an estate tax instead of a succession duty, then I understand the point; but I do not think it has anything to do with jurisdiction. The dominion parliament has jurisdiction to do either or both.

Yes, I
should think it had; I agree with that. But the minister has not apprehended my point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are many who hold the view that we are making a mistake in framing this legislation on the provincial model. There are many who hold the view that we should be imposing a straight graduated estate tax. That would mean that a $10,000 estate would be taxed, let us say for the sake of example, at one per cent; a $20,000 estate at two per cent; a $30,000 estate at three per cent and so on, until you get up to a million dollar estate, which might be taxed at twenty per cent.

That is
the rate of taxation; I was not referring to that at all. I appreciate what the minister is saying about there being some argument for and some advantage in having a graduated tax, but that goes to the rate of taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is graduated, too.

I know it is, in a lesser degree. But what I am pointing out is that primarily a succession duty or death duty tax should be based on the value of the property passing, on the principle of a tax on property, as distinct from a tax on persons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
Well, the minister does not accept that proposal; and I assume, although I have not seen the bill as yet-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What the hon. gentleman
says is not clear.
It is perfectly clear to me. I am sorry I have not been able to make it clear to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not clear to me. The tax imposed by this legislation depends (1) upon the value of the whole estate; (2) upon the value of the property passing to the person taxed, the beneficiary; (3) upon the degree of relationship, whether he is a stranger or otherwise.
Succession Duty Act

That is the incidence of the tax, about which I am not talking. What I am trying to suggest to the minister is that when this tax was first imposed in Canada it was primarily a tax on property. Those who are in the legal profession will recall that this is true; but because of the limited right of taxation vested in the province, which right was confined as the result of a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada and by something said by Chief Justice Anglin in one of his judgments- I have forgotten the name of the case- the amount of property they could tax was restricted. We had the attempt of the province of New Brunswick, at all events, to declare property to be property within the province which was not, in fact, property within the province. I tried to illustrate what I meant by referring to that attempt. Then the provinces shifted their ground, not in order to enlarge their jurisdiction, because that was confined by the constitution, but in order to get at property and values, and to produce results, beyond that which they were able to do on the theory that it was a tax on the property. Now, in most instances, they have attached the tax to the succession to property. I have often thought there was some question about their right to do that where the successor was out of the jurisdiction, but I am not going to argue that point now. The question I am bringing to the attention of the minister is this. The matter of jurisdiction does not enter into it, because the dominion can have any form of taxation it likes; but would it not be better, as a matter of principle, to have the tax imposed on property alone, property passing, rather than what is suggested here? I hope I have made my point clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This tax is on persons.

I regret to have to make the statement to-night that I am strongly opposed to this sort of legislation. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that in the fall of 1935, after the election, a dominion-provincial conference was held, at which the then Minister of Finance mentioned a succession tax to be imposed by the dominion government. That suggestion was made again in the Sirois report. I have tried to read that report, but found it impossible to do so; it is not readable matter. What I could read, after drinking several cups of strong coffee, was the eight-page summary, which contained in a nutshell all the recommendations of that commission. It is time to mention here, sir, what has been very unfairly said by the leader of the opposition; and if he smiles now, his smile will be of short duration. I hold in my hand an extract from the Ottawa Journal 
of January 17 of this year, containing the report of a speech which was made concerning the work of that commission by the horn gentleman in Fredericton. I have always had respect for the dead; but the language used by the leader of the opposition, if not unworthy of him, was unworthy of the high functions of the leader of the great Conservative party of the past, which does not exist any more.
But it will soon.

I remember that my hon. friend presided over two large powwows to select leaders, both of whom are now out of the game although they were great at the time of their selection, one because he was rich and the other because he was cocky. This report states:
The Ottawa conference on dominion-provincial relations ''failed not because of anything the Conservative party had done"-
The Conservative party had done nothing except wrongs.
-"but because of lack of national leadership"-
Hear, hear; national leadership! Think of that!
-"and 'because of a subversive element within the Liberal party"-
What was that subversive element? Can the hon. gentleman name it? Does he dare name it? He remains silent; it is just as well for him.
Speaking to a luncheon meeting of the Albany club, Mr. Hanson told leaders of the Conservative party: "We had an exhibition yesterday within the ranks of the Liberal party that made me blush for my country."
He blushes now because I read his own words. This language, used by the leader of a great party, is an utter shame.
He said that the only man on the original dominion-provincial relations commission who had a working knowledge of Canada's constitution was Hon. N. W. Rowell, who was forced by ill-health to retire from the chairmanship and was succeeded by Dr. J. R. Sirois, of Quebec.
Before Mr. Sirois came to Ottawa I did not know him as a doctor; it is not our practice in Quebec to use that title. He is a man who is very well read in the law; he is familiar with the legislation not only of the province of Quebec but also of Canada. The little I know of law I owe to him. I had great respect for him, more respect than I would have for any Tory, except the hon. member for Broadview.
With regard to the past, remember that the leader of the opposition knows very well what happened when the privy council declared the social legislation he had supported

Succession Duty Act
in this house was declared ultra vires. Then the chairman. Judge Rowell, came to the point where he could say that he could not understand the judgment of the privy council, just because he had been paid $400 a day to defend such legislation before the supreme court. I know whereof I speak, and the hon. member does not know-and does not need to make faces when I speak. I want him to show the dignity that belongs to the position he holds.
Mr. Chairman-
And I do not want interruptions.
I suggest that this speech is entirely out of order.
I am speaking.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A point of order has been taken. Does any other hon. member wish to speak to it?

Yes. In answer to the objection raised by the leader of the opposition, let me say that we are now discussing a resolution concerning succession duties. This measure would take from the provinces part of their power of taxation, in accordance with the suggestions contained in the Rowell-*Sirois commission report, which are familiar to all members in the committee. It is just on that account that I feel I am perfectly in order in mentioning the comment made by the leader of the opposition on precisely the same conclusions of that commission-suggestions which have been made, and which are embodied in these resolutions. When mentioning comments made by the leader of the opposition, I feel I am strictly in order because I express, I repeat, the views he has expressed outside the house, and on the very same matter we are now discussing. That is why I hope the chairman will let me proceed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does any other hon.
member want to speak to the point of order? The resolutions we are studying have to do with succession duties. Resolution 1 embodies the principle of levying duties on successions in Canada. Section 2 of standing order 58 reads:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
It is permissible in discussing this matter, which has also been the subject of an investigation by the Sirois commission, to make brief references to the Sirois report. But inasmuch as standing order 58, section 2, restricts the discussion strictly to the resolution now under discussion, it would be out of order to develop a general discussion on the principles
involved, because those principles should have been discussed when the budget speech was under advisement, and was being discussed.
To follow the rules of the house we must now limit discussion strictly to the resolution before the committee. My ruling is that although a brief reference to the principles studied, discussed and reported upon by the Sirois report is permissible in a discussion of this resolution, I am afraid the hon. member went beyond the proper limit of that latitude when he made reference to speeches made outside the house by the leader of the opposition. I would draw the hon. member's attention to the necessity to limiting his remarks strictly to the resolution before the committee.
Yes, sir. I will put this clipping in my pocket.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not believe that
the hon. member, if I heard him aright, with proper respect for the chairman, can say, that he will put that ruling in his pocket. I think the hon. member ought to adhere to the ruling, and observe the rules of the house.

I did not intend to use any disrespectful language. I was just abiding by Mr. Chairman's ruling. If he took what I said in a different way, then I am very sorry;
I did not mean it at all in that way. It was just a way of expressing myself, to tell him that I was abiding by his decision.
I find this one of the most serious matters which may be brought to the attention of the committee. Of course we have a system of taxation which dates back to confederation. It was only after lengthy argument that the provinces agreed to depart from a certain number of rights of taxation, in favour of the new organization, which was the Dominion of Canada. You know, sir, because I am sure you have read the confederation debates, how difficult the matter was. When I think of the great political ancestors of the present Minister of Finance, and of those who were so strongly in favour of equal rights for all the provinces-and not only that, but equal rights for the provinces and for the dominion -I find that this piece of legislation is very dangerous. I will say why, in a moment.
There is, of course, a belief among people that the order of precedence in Canada replaces the British North America Act. I must explain myself. If any one of us attends a state funeral, or any state occasion where the precedence list is followed, he will see the representatives of the dominion in the first place, and then will follow in turn the representatives of the provinces. The same thing applies to the seating in this house. At the present time, Mr. Chairman, you occupy
Succession Duty Act

the chair. Therefore you are superior to the Prime Minister; you are superior to any one of his colleagues in this house; you are superior to the leader of the opposition, or the leader of any other group; you are superior to every hon. member. There are treasury benches because the 244 other members cannot all sit in the same seat. The seats must be distributed in order that there may be some order. Therefore, we have the Prime Minister; we have his colleagues; we have the leader of the opposition and the other members. It is the same thing with regard to the provinces. Everybody cannot walk on the same line; everybody must walk in turn. According to the British North America Act which I hold/ in my hand, the premier of each province who came here, the Premier of Prince Edward Island, the smallest in Canada, and the Premier of Ontario, the largest in Canada, were all on an equal footing with the Prime Minister of Canada. They were here to discuss the British North America Act, the constitution of our country.
The reason why that is so is the fact that the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction in certain matters. The legislatures of the provinces are the sovereign masters regarding legislation within the provinces. The dominion parliament is its own boss in matters in which it has exclusive jurisdiction. This is the system to which the people have been accustomed for scores of years. The dominion parliament, by subsection 3 of section 91 of the British North America Act, is given the power to raise money by any method of taxation. In a sense, I may be answered by the Minister of Finance that this legislation of his is intra vires. That may be so. There is another factor to consider. A practice has been in force since confederation, not only in Ottawa but in the provinces, to levy taxation in certain fields.
The provinces are the bosses of their destinies in their own fields. Another most important matter is the fact that certain things have been done for the people of this country by the dominion parliament, many of which were of interest to several of the provinces. On the other hand, however, the provinces have done other things. They have set up their own staffs and have been doing these things since confederation. The organization exists; the wheels have been greased, and this work has been carried on quite well since confederation. This is being done in connection with colonization, agriculture, and especially unemployment. The provinces have been accustomed to doing certain things necessary for the welfare of the people. This was done

by the little communities, the municipalities, and by the larger communities, the provinces. Sometimes the provinces had to come to Ottawa for support.
Take, for instance, unemployment. We all know the large amounts of money that were collected by the provinces through succession duties. I can understand why the Tories of Ontario are mad because of the succession duties they were forced to pay by Mr. Hepburn. They had to pay large sums of money into the exchequer of the province, and they were quite dissatisfied with the way in which that collection was made in the public interest. But it was necessary for the province of Ontario, and much good resulted. The same applies to the province of Quebec and other provinces.
It is pretty hard to think that the dominion government is taking the power of taxation in connection with succession duties from the provinces and is at the same time refusing to contribute to the support of the unemployed. In my province five per cent of the population is unemployed, and yet the province is deprived of assistance from succession duties. They expect to receive some help from Ottawa, but Ottawa says "no." I protest against it. I cannot be in favour of this legislation. It is impossible for me; my conscience objects to it when I think of the poor people who will suffer because of this legislation. I am not considering these matters from the legal point of view; I am looking at them from the practical point of view. I cannot agree with this legislation when I consider what the results will be. My conscience does not permit me to agree with it. I know that the language I use now will receive the support of the people of any constituency in this country.
I cannot conceive how this government can take this power away from the provinces and then not give some help in caring for the unemployed, especially when the unemployed have been cared for partly by means of money received by the provinces from succession duties. I protest most strongly against this legislation. Who was behind the scheme which was forced upon the Minister of Finance? I do not mean this one; I do not mean the other one; I mean the one before that. What is the mystery about that scheme which was suggested- in 1935? These people come again with these schemes. I warn the minister that it is dangerous and that we live in hard times. While the ministers in Ottawa may be good-hearted, they do not come in contact

Succession Duty Act
with the people in the same way that members of parliament do who go home for the week-end.
When I go home over the week-end, from fifty to eighty people from all walks of life talk to me and tell me their troubles. As I said last year, they honour me by opening up their hearts. They tell me their troubles and I try to help them, but a member of parliament cannot help all the people who need it. There must be some outside help. Unemployment is not cured as yet, and the provinces should be given some help. They cannot pay any more. The financial scissors of Ottawa have passed through their budgets, and the people will have to suffer. There is no reason for this even in war time. People are sick, people are willing to work, but are unable to find it. The reports of the Department of Labour are all wrong if they say that in this total war effort we have total employment. We should have, but we have not. The provinces have to support these poor people and they have not the means to do so.
I hope the minister will reconsider this legislation. This is one of the most serious matters because it affects the health and lives of a large number of our compatriots. They deserve help; they need help, and they should get it, either from Ottawa or from the provinces. If Ottawa takes over the powers which the provinces have in order to sustain them, what will happen? We have this case. I am against centralization. This is a case of centralization. As a Liberal I am against it; it means nothing good to me I am in favour of decentralization, which is one of the main principles of Liberalism, just as much as free speech and so forth. Therefore I appeal to the Minister of Finance and to the government to reconsider this part of their taxation programme. It is not a question of winning. There was a tie here at this table in January, but it is not a question whether the minister shall win. It is not a question of winning or not winning, on the part of the minister, any more than it is on the part of the premiers of the provinces. It is a question of coming to a settlement which will not make people suffer, which will be fair to all and which will enable this government to carry on the pursuit of war without exposing any number of our fellow citizens to death from hunger.

Before the hon. member
resumes his seat, I should like to know whether, when he makes such criticism of the proposals with regard to succession duties, he has in mind that the policy of the present
government is to refund to the provinces the amount actually collected by each province in that field.

I thank my hon. friend
for his interruption; it will permit me to explain more fully what I have to say. If the government is to collect these succession taxes and give them back to the provinces, what is the use of this legislation? If this legislation does not take any power of taxation from the provinces, how is it that the provinces have decided to curtail the help they are giving to the unemployed? I cannot understand it, but the minister will have ample opportunity to explain it. In the first place, if the legislation does not take any power from the provinces how is it that the provinces have to curtail their assistance to the unemployed? That is one question. Another is this. If the dominion government is to give back to the provinces the money they will collect through this legislation, what is the use of having this legislation? These are things I cannot understand, and I warn the minister that this is very dangerous.
When there is a certain order that has been established, war is no reason for changing it completely in this way, and the consequence may be quite serious in the aftermath, when we have to settle problems of returned men, the problem of unemployment following the war, and so on. All that will be most difficult, and the dominion government will have to go to the provinces again and ask for help, after having taken some powers from them.
It may be that I am a traditionalist, but I believe in respecting tradition and not changing what is going well. Besides that, I warn the minister against university professors. He is a practical man. He has lived among the people. Let him be very careful in his dealings with those who are book-worms, who are trying to make experimentations on a large scale. He knows very well that Claude Bernard, the great chemist, Lord Lister and Pasteur all experimented on the infinitely small, with a microscope, and then they enlarged their experiments until they were sure they were scientifically correct. Here it is different. Wherever an experiment is made it is dominion-wide. If it is good, so much the better; everyone will prosper. If it is bad, everyone may suffer. It is important to have the popular reaction to every one of these tests. I should like someone to proceed scientifically in these matters, and then we would realize how difficult it is to make any change of this scope in taxation. It is like the wheels of a watch. The watch keeps
Succession Duty Act

time, provided the wheels are in the right place; but if you change the wheels, the watch may go faster or slower or it may not go at all. It is a serious matter, and since it is eleven o'clock now I may say something to-morrow.

Has the minister determined when this tax will be payable? If not, may I suggest that he make it payable after letters of administration or probate issue in the particular provinces. In view of the fact that the provinces have complete control over property and civil rights, they can hold up the issue indefinitely, prevent the executors from handling the property and thus prevent payment of the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will consider that.
May we have an explanation from the minister as to whether it is a refund or an indemnity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The terms of the offer to the provinces are that the dominion is prepared to pay to the provinces the amount of income tax and corporation tax collected by the provinces in the fiscal year which ends nearest January 1, 1941, but not the amount of the succession duty. The succession duty is on a different basis. The dominion will collect this succession duty, and the provinces will continue in the succession duty field as well, if they wish, and collect and keep their own succession duties. They are not disturbed in the collection of succession duties by this legislation.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, May 20, 1941.
